title: Between Shiva and the Jina
subtitle: Shaiva Stones, Jaina Copper: The Twin Paths of Kadamba Power
moral: A durable culture can honor more than one sacred path.

sources.citation: Halasi copper plates of Kakusthavarma and Mrigeshavarma; Fleet (1877), Desai (1957), Gai (1996)
sources.note: Jain invocation Jayati Bhagavan Jinendra and Jain donations.

sources.citation: Talagunda pillar inscription; Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906)
sources.note: Shaiva invocation, genealogy and temple-tank context.

sources.citation: P.B. Desai, Jainism in South India and Some Jaina Epigraphs (1957); Vilas Sangave, Jainism in Karnataka (1981); Upinder Singh (2016)
sources.note: Religious pluralism and Jain patronage debate.

panels.shot: wide, slightly low-angle interior of a royal hall split visually: one side with a linga shrine, the other with a seated Jina image, the Kadamba Royal Patron between them

dialogue.text: In Banavasi, the Kadamba kings praised Shiva in stone and the Jina in copper, building a kingdom not of one faith, but of many.

panels.shot: epic bird's-eye over Banavasi town with river, fields and temple spires, early morning mist

dialogue.text: In the fourth century, when the Kadambas rose in Banavasi, this forest town became a stage where old Vedic lines met new paths of faith.

panels.shot: slow push-in on the Talagunda pillar standing near a tank, with Kadamba Royal Patron in the middle ground, contemplative

dialogue.text: At Talagunda, a stone pillar remembers their pride: Manavya-gotra Brahmanas, dharmamaharajas, guardians of tanks, temples and lineage.

panels.shot: medium close-up on Kadamba Royal Patron seated with Brahmana scribes, palm-leaf manuscripts in front, interior hall

dialogue.text: Their public face was clear: Brahmanical kings, rooted in gotra and dharma, shaping a landscape of shrines and tanks to mirror their order.

panels.shot: low-angle wide shot of a Shaiva temple courtyard, with Kadamba Royal Patron overseeing artisans placing a linga

dialogue.text: Madhukeshvara, Praneshvara: names of Shiva that clung to Kadamba stones, as shrines rose and bells folded the land into Shaiva sound.

panels.shot: tight close-up on a copper plate charter being unrolled by the king’s hand, engraved letters catching the light

dialogue.text: Yet at Halasi, the same court unrolled copper that began not with Shiva, but with a different praise: Jayati Bhagavan Jinendra.

panels.shot: medium shot of Kadamba Royal Patron listening to a Jain acharya in a simple mandapa, contrast with royal ornaments

dialogue.speaker: kadamba_patrons
dialogue.text: Your path is gentle, acharya. Our land must learn to hold many paths.

panels.shot: wide shot of a donation ceremony at Halasi: king granting land, Jain monks and officials present

dialogue.text: Kakusthavarma’s plates speak of Jina first, then of land and rights, marking Halasi as a place where Jain teachers found royal shelter.

panels.shot: split-depth shot: foreground Jain monks teaching, background Shaiva priests at a temple, both within the same townscape

dialogue.text: Palasika, Halasi, Banavasi: the records show Jina shrines near Shiva temples, Jain acharyas and Shaiva priests walking the same dusty streets.

panels.shot: interior court scene, slightly high angle, showing multiple groups: Brahmana ritualists, Jain monks, royal counselors

dialogue.text: Some scholars call them Shaiva, some Jain, some simply Brahmanical kings. The inscriptions refuse a simple story of one conversion and one creed.

panels.shot: medium close-up on the king in quiet debate with two advisors representing different traditions, candlelight casting long shadows

dialogue.speaker: kadamba_patrons
dialogue.text: Our duty is rajadharma. Let it not be narrowed by one banner.

panels.shot: dynamic oblique view of scribes engraving different invocations on separate plates, piles of copper sheets around

dialogue.text: One grant to a Shaiva temple, another to a Jain sangha: the Kadamba chancery learned to switch invocations as easily as it moved from forest to field.

panels.shot: wide dusk shot of Banavasi with both temple shikharas and simple Jain basadi roofs visible, smoke rising

dialogue.text: From c. 345 to 540, under Kadamba rule, the town’s sacred map thickened: Shaiva spires, Jain halls, ponds that served all.

panels.shot: subtle low-angle on Kadamba Royal Patron walking along a temple tank embankment, reflecting in the water with both shrines in the background

dialogue.text: Their pillar at Talagunda remembers a tank beside a temple, but their copper from Halasi remembers Jina first; together they hint at a policy of layered patronage.

panels.shot: intercut-style composition: ghosted overlays of later dynasties and Xuanzang’s imagined visit, with Kadamba king as a faint earlier layer

dialogue.text: Centuries later, Xuanzang saw Buddhist Banavasi, but his report belongs to another age; the Kadambas’ record is Shaiva-Jain, not a hidden Buddhist kingdom.

panels.shot: close-up on weathered hands of a modern researcher holding rubbings of inscriptions, overlays of ancient script visible

dialogue.text: Today, historians read their pillars and plates and find no single faith-flag to raise, only a pattern of support that shifted with place, purpose and audience.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide shot: ruins and standing temples at Banavasi and Halasi under a vast sky, tiny human figures walking between

dialogue.text: Between Shiva and the Jina, the Kadambas learned that a kingdom can endure not by one sacred path alone, but by holding many in its shadow.
